claims.text: Lippan kaam, or mud and mirror work, is a traditional mural craft of Kutch that is also called Chittar Kaam.

quotes.quote: Mud and mirror work is known as Lipan Kaam. It is a traditional mural craft of Kutch. It is also called as Chittar Kaam.
The traditional mud mirror art which is also known as Lippan Kaam or Chittar Kaam is one of the overlooked marvellous arts that India offers.

claims.text: The mud mirror work of Kutch, Gujarat, locally known as Lippan Kaam, is renowned for its intricate motifs and aesthetic appeal.

quotes.quote: the mud mirror work of Kutch, Gujarat - locally known as Lippan Kaam - is renowned for its intricate motifs and aesthetic appeal.

claims.text: Lippan is used to embellish the interior and exterior walls of the circular adobes, locally known as bhungas, in which its communities live.

quotes.quote: It is used to embellish the interior and exterior walls of the circular adobes i.e. locally Known as "Bhungas" that these communities live in.

claims.text: Lippan is practised mainly by the Rabari, Kumbhar, Marwada Harijan and Mutwa communities.

quotes.quote: Lippan is practiced mainly by the Rabari, Kumbhar, Marwada Harijan and Mutwa communities
Apart from the Kumbhars, the Rabari, Mutwa, and Marwada communities also partake in lippan.

quotes.locator: A Craft Rooted in the Sands of Time
quotes.quote: The craft is primarily practiced by the once nomadic Rabari, Kumbhar, Marwada Harijan, and Mutwa communities, each of whom has shaped its evolution.

claims.text: A Press Information Bureau feature of September 2023 says most lippan artisans trace their origins to the Kumbhar community.

quotes.quote: but most Lippan artisans today trace their origins to the Kumbhar community.
10 Sep, 2023 G20 is a significant event which is altering the way the world looks at India.

claims.text: In local Gujarati the word lippan means clay or dung, and kaam means work.

quotes.quote: The word "Lippan' means 'clay' or 'dung' in local Gujarati, and the word 'kaam' denotes 'work'.
lippan translates to 'dung' or 'clay' in the local dialect

claims.text: The origins of lippan kaam are unknown, and the distinct styles of the different Kutch communities make its roots even harder to trace.

quotes.quote: The origins of Lipan Kaam are unknown. Various communities in Kutch do mud-relief work and have their own distinct style of lipan kaam. This makes it even harder to trace the roots of Lipan Kaam.

quotes.locator: A Craft Rooted in the Sands of Time
quotes.quote: The origins of Lippan Art remain elusive, buried in the oral traditions of Kutch's desert communities.

claims.text: The art form is believed to come from the Kumbhar potters of Sindh, who moved it from pots to the inner and outer walls of homes.

quotes.quote: The art form seems to have come to be because of the Kumbhar community who were earthen pot-makers from Sindh. From pots, they moved the art form to larger canvases such as interior and exterior walls of homes.

quotes.locator: A Craft Rooted in the Sands of Time
quotes.quote: The Kumbhar community, originally potters from Sindh, is believed to have adapted their skills to architectural surfaces, decorating walls with sculpted mud motifs.

claims.text: Mud and mirror work has been in practice for centuries.

quotes.quote: For centuries, this captivating craft adorned the interior walls of homes, not only for its aesthetic appeal but also for its ability to keep interiors cool during the scorching summer months.
This three dimensional mirror inlaid mud work, which has been in practice for centuries, is now on the verge of being lost

claims.text: Outlook Traveller reported the mirror-inlaid mud work on the verge of being lost because modern families tend to plaster their homes with cement.

quotes.quote: This three dimensional mirror inlaid mud work, which has been in practice for centuries, is now on the verge of being lost because modern families tend to plaster their homes with cement.

claims.text: Homegrown reports that lippan was in decline until 2005, when the launch of the Rann Utsav brought the art and its artists recognition.

quotes.quote: The art was on a journey of decline until 2005, when the Rann Utsav was launched. Here, the art and the artists gained much-deserved recognition and appreciation.
In 2005, the launch of the Rann Utsav, a festival celebrating the crafts of Kutch, further propelled Lippan Art into the mainstream.

claims.text: The Hans India reports that the art regained its significance because artisans showed their work to people through social media platforms.

quotes.quote: However, currently, the art has regained its significance due to artisans who unveiled their ethnic works to the people through social media platforms.

quotes.quote: Around 2021-22, this art has become quite popular and artists have started experimenting with the readily available clay & mirrors.

quotes.quote: Earlier, with the unavailability of pre-cut mirrors, a large mirror would be shattered using stones, and the pieces would then be collected to use in the lippan.

claims.text: Lippan begins with a dough of dung and clay; a border called kaam or kaamtane is made, the dough is laid onto the pattern and mirrors are added.

quotes.quote: The process begins with making a dough-like mixture of dung and clay which can be laid onto a flat surface such as walls.
After a border, called kaam or kaamtane, is made, this dough is rolled out as desired and laid onto the pattern. Then, the addition of mirrors takes place.

claims.text: The paste is rolled into long cylindrical shapes, moulded by hand and attached to the walls in geometric shapes, which are then inlaid with tiny mirrors.

quotes.quote: is then rolled into long cylindrical shapes, moulded by hand and attached to the walls into geometric shapes. The patterns are then inlaid with tiny mirrors.

claims.text: After it is decorated with mirrors, lippan work takes days to dry before it is coloured.

quotes.quote: Finally, it is decorated with mirrors to provide the contrasting texture of the clay and produce intricate designs that are coloured later. It takes days to dry before they are coloured.

claims.text: According to AIACA, a lippan art piece takes 2-7 days to make and involves 1-2 artisans.

quotes.locator: How much time does it take
quotes.quote: A Lippan Art piece takes 2-7 days, involving 1-2 artisans in the process

claims.text: Clay relief work in Kutch is carried out using brushes made from branches of the baval tree.

quotes.quote: the process is carried out using brushes made from branches of the baval tree.

claims.text: Lippan is also the traditional technique of applying a fine clay paste, finer than that of the walls, over bhunga floors of silt, cattle dung and water.

quotes.quote: The floor of the Bhunga is constructed using the same materials as the walls: silt, cattle dung, and water, layered one over the other. This traditional technique is known as Lippan, where a fine paste of clay, finer than that used in the walls, is applied.

claims.text: The Lippan floor plaster is applied with a semicircular motion of the hands, repeated twice to three times a year depending on wear and tear.

quotes.quote: The process involves a semicircular motion of the hands to apply the plaster, which is repeated twice to three times a year, depending on wear and tear.

claims.text: Repeated Lippan plastering helps insulate the house and disinfect surfaces after the monsoon, and raises the structure a few centimetres each cycle against dusty winds.

quotes.quote: This repeated plaster application helps insulate the house and disinfect the surfaces following the monsoon season. Additionally, the re-plastering process incrementally elevates the structure by a few centimetres with each cycle, protecting from the dusty winds prevalent in the settlement.

claims.text: Kutch bhungas are built of clay or bamboo chips plastered with lipan, a mixture of clay and dung, under wooden-based thatched roofs.

lede.text: Lippan kaam, or mud and mirror work, is a traditional mural craft of Kutch, also called Chittar Kaam, renowned for its intricate motifs.
It embellishes the interior and exterior walls of the circular adobes known as bhungas, and is practised mainly by the Rabari, Kumbhar, Marwada Harijan and Mutwa communities.
A dough of dung and clay is laid onto a pattern and mirrors are added, and the work takes days to dry before it is coloured.

sentences.text: The origins of lippan kaam are unknown, and the distinct styles of different Kutch communities make its roots even harder to trace.
Mud and mirror work has been in practice for centuries.
The Press Information Bureau describes the Mutva community as one of the oldest custodians of lippan kaam.
Before pre-cut mirrors were available, a large mirror was shattered with stones and the pieces collected for lippan.

Sources differ on whether the craft is still declining: Homegrown reports that the art was in decline until 2005, when the launch of the Rann Utsav brought it recognition, while Outlook Traveller reported the mirror-inlaid mud work on the verge of being lost because modern families tend to plaster their homes with cement.
The Hans India reports that the art regained its significance because artisans showed their work through social media platforms, and that around 2021-22 lippan became quite popular.
The process begins with a dough of dung and clay, after which a border called kaam or kaamtane is made and the dough is laid onto the pattern.
The paste is rolled into long cylindrical shapes, moulded by hand and attached to the walls in geometric shapes, which are then inlaid with tiny mirrors.
After it is decorated with mirrors, the work takes days to dry before it is coloured.
According to AIACA, a piece takes 2-7 days and involves 1-2 artisans.
Lippan also names a fine clay paste applied to bhunga floors with a semicircular motion of the hands, twice to three times a year, depending on wear and tear.
AIACA lists the raw materials as local clay or mud, animal dung blended with the clay, and small polished mirrors or glass pieces.
Sources differ on the dung: camel dung in Ramdevnagar, camel or wild ass dung as the binding agent, donkey dung in one artist's account, and fibrous horse manure in Outlook Traveller's report.
Millet is sometimes used as an alternative, to prevent the attraction of termites.
AIACA lists coarse sand and fine straw or fibre as added to reduce shrinkage, and natural pigments with lime or gypsum for white highlights.
The lippan dough has evolved: many artisans use clay, chalk powder, sawdust and glue instead of dung and clay, to make the art longer-lasting and odour-free.
The most popular designs in Kutch are geometric shapes and forms, peacocks, camels, mango trees, symbolic temples and daily activities of life.
A lippan artist told The Hans India that the communities whose walls it adorns have similar designs and motifs in their embroideries.
AIACA gives the colours as ochres, whites and browns, while contemporary pieces used bright turquoise, red and green with black outlines.
Clay relief work in Kutch also constructs kotholo granaries, sanjiro stores, kothi grain stores, dhadablo baby seats, chula hearths and paniyara platforms.
In Kutch, mud granaries are made by women, who decorate them with mud-relief and mirror work.
Lippan adorned the interior walls of homes not only for its aesthetic appeal but also for its ability to keep interiors cool in the scorching summer months.
Repeated Lippan plastering of the floors helps insulate the house and disinfect surfaces after the monsoon.
In Ramdevnagar, natural materials maintain cool interiors, vital for survival in Kutch's scorching heat.
In Hodko village, Kutch, master artisan Bharmabehn's home preserves a splendid display of Kutchi mud work, Outlook Traveller reported.
In the Ramdevnagar cluster of Bhirandiara village in Kutch, women practise lippan art alongside embroidery, jewellery making, beadwork and toy making.
Kothi granaries decorated with mud-relief and mirror work are recorded at Bhujodi and at Gandhi Nu Gam in Kutch.
A lippan artist from Bhopal who began in 2010 has conducted workshops on mud and mirror art, both offline and online.
Kutch Art Trust, Samtra filed Geographical Indication application 1768 for Kutch Lippan (Mud Mirror) Craft of Gujarat on 31 December 2025.
The registry lists it at pre-examination, while AIACA's page states that lippan art received a GI tag in 2023.
Lippan has found a new place in interior design as wall decor, made in frames or on wooden panels.
